clue.text: Recreations in father's paper

parts.note: father is PA, and with the possessive becomes PA'S
The Times is the newspaper

explanation.surface: Dad's hobbies are all found in his newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobbies and games are things that pass the time, which is what recreations are.

clue.text: Stuff cut on southern fields

parts.note: to pad is to stuff or fill out
to dock is to cut short, as a tail

explanation.surface: Filling trimmed from the southern side of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Small enclosed grazing grounds for horses are called by this name.

clue.text: Feeling able to give opinion

definitions.meaning: a view held, as in 'my ... exactly'

explanation.surface: Feeling capable of offering one's view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'able to give' is a link: the one word can stand for either sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both an emotion and a view one holds about something.

clue.text: End of a cold season, meaning that of an archbishopric

indicators.note: the tail of the word is kept: all but its opening letter

parts.note: winter is the cold season

explanation.surface: A churchman's ending at the close of winter.
explanation.walkthrough: The end of WINTER is INTER; the end of the archbishopric of Canterbury is BURY, and to bury is to inter. 'meaning' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Canterbury, the senior archbishop's see, ends in a word for laying a body in the grave.

clue.text: East gets Doctor Rowe materials to put among the foliage

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree

indicators.note: the name is raw material to be worked into a new shape, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An Eastern doctor gathers garden supplies to hide something in the leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'materials' plays on raw materials: the name Rowe is the stuff to be reworked into OWER.
explanation.definitionFit: To shelter something within a leafy arbour is to set it in among the leaves.

clue.text: This month lasts a year

parts.note: the last month of the calendar arrives once the whole year has run, and by number December is the final one of the dozen

explanation.surface: A complaint that the current month drags on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: December is month number twelve, the month that closes the year; 'lasts' means comes last as well as goes on.
explanation.definitionFit: December, the year's final month, is month number twelve in the calendar.

clue.text: Standard yields ?

parts.note: a standard is a banner, and this one is the banner that signals surrender

explanation.surface: Asking how much produce a normal crop gives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard yields' reads like normal crop returns; a standard is a flag, and 'yields' means surrenders.
explanation.definitionFit: The pale banner raised by a side giving up is the flag of surrender.

clue.text: Clear clue eliminated church, detectives conclude

indicators.note: the detectives come at the close, ending the word
the church's letters are knocked out of the word clue

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British police detectives

explanation.surface: A plain hint ruled out the church, the police decide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eliminated' takes CE out of CLUE, leaving LU; 'conclude' puts CID last. CID is the UK detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucid writing is clear and easy to follow.

clue.text: Perhaps Amelia's morning off work

parts.note: take the morning, AM, off the name to leave Elia's, and the Elia works by Charles Lamb are the famous prose pieces

explanation.surface: A woman named Amelia may be taking the morning off from her job.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing AM (morning) from AMELIA'S leaves ELIA'S, recalling Charles Lamb's 'Essays of Elia', a classic English prose collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamb's famous book of Elia pieces is a collection of short prose compositions.

clue.text: Underground workers turn up round Land's End ? Not often

indicators.note: the turned word wraps around the other letter
in a down clue turning up means reading the word from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: moles tunnel and work under the ground

indicators.note: the end of the word Land, its last letter

explanation.surface: Miners rarely surface near the tip of Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn up' reverses MOLES to SELOM; 'round' wraps it about D, the 'End' of Land's. Land's End is the far tip of Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens rarely happens not often.

clue.text: Try to get money from horses in Bedfordshire

parts.note: to dun is to press a debtor for payment
a stable is a set of racehorses kept by one owner

explanation.surface: Someone chasing a debt from a horse yard in the Home Counties.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedfordshire is an English county north of London, and Dunstable is one of its towns.
explanation.definitionFit: The defining phrase names a location: the town lies in that English county.

clue.text: Indians can sit endlessly in assembly

indicators.note: the letters are put together afresh, assembled into a new order
the word sit loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Native people are allowed to keep sitting in a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assembly' looks like a meeting hall but is the signal to put the letters together anew; 'endlessly' trims the second word before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca people of Peru are American Indians in the older sense of the word.

clue.text: Basket maker in Cheshire is on point of retiring

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the concealed letters are read from right to left
the letters sit inside the run of words Cheshire is on

explanation.surface: A craftsman in north-west England is about to give up work.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'cheshiRE IS On' backwards ('retiring') gives the willow; 'point of' is padding. Cheshire is a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Willow shoots of this kind are the material basket weavers use, so the plant makes baskets.

clue.text: One of seven associated with Sheffield

definitions.meaning: one of the days of the week
Sheffield's football club carries this day in its name

explanation.surface: Something connected with Sheffield that is one of a group of seven.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheffield Wednesday is an English football club from the city of Sheffield.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the week's seven days, and it is also the name of Sheffield's older football club.

clue.text: Artist makes toll-call ?

definitions.meaning: Sir Godfrey ..., court portrait painter to several English monarchs
one who sounds a funeral bell, a knell, read as a doer noun ending -ER

explanation.surface: A painter rings up and pays for the call.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the name as KNELL plus -ER: one who tolls a bell. 'Toll-call' suggests a paid phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: Kneller was a famous portrait painter; split up, the name is a bell-ringer who sounds the death bell.

clue.text: Riches and clothes raised for Roman poet

parts.note: lucre is money, wealth

indicators.note: in a down clue raising a word turns it upside down, read backwards

parts.note: a suit is a set of clothes

explanation.surface: A wealthy Roman poet's wardrobe is lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' reverses SUIT to TIUS under LUCRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucretius wrote the Latin philosophical poem De Rerum Natura.

clue.text: A bluestocking's complaint ?

parts.note: a bluestocking is a learned woman, one with an MA (Master of Arts)
the learned woman is a lady with a degree

explanation.surface: Asking what a learned woman might grumble about.
explanation.walkthrough: A bluestocking is an educated woman: an MA LADY. 'Complaint' reads as a grievance but means an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: An illness or ailment is often called a complaint in medical language.

clue.text: Resolve to take courses about meter-adjustment

indicators.note: the meal word goes around the other letters

parts.note: to dine is to eat a meal of several courses

indicators.note: adjusting the meter changes its letters about

explanation.surface: A promise to go on courses about fixing a meter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolve' looks like a noun beside 'to take courses', but it is the verb; 'adjustment' scrambles the meter and 'about' wraps the meal round it.
explanation.definitionFit: To resolve is to decide firmly, settle on a course.

clue.text: Challenging article run by old military offender

definitions.meaning: the armoured glove thrown down as a challenge
a soldier being punished had to run between two rows of men who struck him

explanation.surface: A defiant newspaper piece written by a former army criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: To throw down the glove was to challenge; 'running the gauntlet' was an old military punishment between lines of men.
explanation.definitionFit: The armoured glove is both the challenge token and, in the phrase, the double file of men an offender had to run between.

clue.text: Bloomers fitted round legs ?

definitions.meaning: flowers: the stock is a garden flower
the old punishment frame clamped round the ankles, or stockings

explanation.surface: Ladies' knickers that fit snugly round the thighs.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers suggests underwear but means plants that bloom. The pillory-like frame held offenders by the legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock is a scented garden flower, and a wooden frame that held an offender by the ankles had the same name.

clue.text: Pen-name of some service ?

definitions.meaning: the author H. C. McNeile of the Bulldog Drummond stories wrote under this name
a soldier of the Royal Engineers, a branch of the armed services

explanation.surface: Asking the writing name of someone useful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of some service' reads as 'useful' but means a member of an armed service, the military engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: McNeile's writing name was also the army word for a combat engineer, a member of a service.

clue.text: Meeting attended by crafty types

parts.note: crafty here means owning craft, i.e. boats, so the gathering is one for boats and those who sail them

explanation.surface: A gathering full of cunning schemers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crafty' suggests cunning; here it means people in boats (craft).
explanation.definitionFit: A race meeting for rowing or sailing boats is a gathering of small craft and their crews.

clue.text: Part of rigging used by sailor up Nile, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue the word is written upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor

indicators.note: perhaps signals a possible variant, the river's letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Rigging used by a seaman going up the Nile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses TAR to RAT; 'perhaps' rearranges NILE to LINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratlines are the small ropes across the shrouds that make a ladder up a ship's rigging.

clue.text: Sheriff's men take opener for drink

parts.note: a posse is a band of men summoned by a sheriff

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Deputies have a first round of drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A posset is an old hot drink of milk curdled with ale or wine.

clue.text: Black's place is taken immediately

definitions.meaning: in snooker the black ball sits on its marked spot on the table

explanation.surface: A chess or snooker player's position is occupied at once.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker each coloured ball has a marked spot on the table; when the black is respotted it is put back there.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something there and then means doing it at once, without moving away.

clue.text: Article about an old noble

indicators.note: the article goes around the other word

parts.note: the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A piece of writing about an aristocrat from history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' could be any piece of writing; here it is the grammatical article, and 'about' wraps it round the other word.
explanation.definitionFit: A thane was an Anglo-Saxon or Scottish lord, like Macbeth.

clue.text: Fool has no right to order retreat

indicators.note: to retreat is to go backwards, so the assembled letters are read right to left

parts.note: OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: A fool lacks any entitlement to command a withdrawal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreat' reads the whole string backwards; 'has' and 'to' are link words. 'order' looks like a command but is the honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are insults for someone stupid, a dimwit or idiot.

clue.text: Native suggests art master as an alternative to himself

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts
or offers an alternative
speaking of himself a person says I

explanation.surface: An indigenous man proposes an art teacher could stand in for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suggests' is the link; 'himself' is the native's own word for himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maori are the indigenous people of New Zealand.

clue.text: Hindu teacher gives quarters to friend abroad

parts.note: S for south, one compass point or quarter
W for west, another compass quarter
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: A guru offers lodgings to a foreign pal.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points are 'quarters'; two of them, S and W, come first.
explanation.definitionFit: A swami is a Hindu religious master or guru.

clue.text: Leader might be one of 8?

parts.note: a newspaper leader is a leading article, and 8 down is a set of short prose pieces, of which this kind of article is one

explanation.surface: A captain might be one of a group of eight, like a rowing crew.
explanation.walkthrough: Leader is the British term for a newspaper's opinion piece; 8 down's answer is short prose pieces, which such a piece is.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's leading article giving its own opinion is a short prose composition.

clue.text: Belief is embraced by them

indicators.note: being embraced means being held inside, so one word goes within the other

explanation.surface: A conviction that they hold dear.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the wordplay share the surface: 'them' holding 'is' is the belief they hold.
explanation.definitionFit: Belief in a god or gods is the doctrine meant here, the opposite of atheism.

clue.text: Met Denis wandering in the grounds

indicators.note: the letters stray from their places, rearranged

explanation.surface: Bumped into Denis strolling round the estate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandering' rearranges MET and DENIS; 'grounds' looks like an estate but means dregs.
explanation.definitionFit: Coffee grounds are the dregs that settle to the bottom, a deposit.
